messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Detective Marcus Taufa

Marcus Taufa was fifty-six years old when he first came to the clinic, though the detective's bearing—shoulders perpetually braced, jaw clenched—made him seem older. He had worked homicide for twenty-eight years, and in that time had built a reputation for methodical patience and an almost preternatural ability to read crime scenes. His colleagues did not know that this gift was rooted in something darker: the permanent vigilance instilled in him as a child, when his stepfather's rages had taught him to read the smallest shifts in tone and posture as matters of survival.

The abuse had been sporadic and savage. Marcus was eight when it began, and by twelve he had learned to monitor his stepfather's breathing, the particular shuffle of his boots across the kitchen tile, the smell of burnt tobacco that preceded the worst of it. The violence was not frequent enough to be predictable, but constant enough that Marcus could never fully relax. His stepfather would disappear into rages over nothing—a meal prepared wrong, a look misinterpreted—and the boy would find himself pinned against a wall, gasping, certain he would not survive. He did survive, but something in him remained in that moment, waiting for the next blow.

For decades, Marcus had channeled this hypervigilance into police work. The job felt like home in a way nothing else did—a place where constant alertness was not pathology but professional virtue. He married, divorced, moved through his career with quiet competence. But three years ago, during a particularly brutal homicide investigation, something had broken. The victim was a young man, Samoan like Marcus, with the same broad shoulders and dark eyes. The crime scene photographs triggered something primal: Marcus found himself unable to look at the images without his body flooding with panic, his heart hammering as though he were the one in danger. When he finally closed the case, he thought the reaction would fade. It did not.

Instead, Marcus began to notice that certain things in the world had become dangerous in ways he could not fully articulate. The smell of burnt tobacco—once merely a sensory memory—now sent him into a state of acute alarm, his body tensing as though threat were imminent. When he encountered men who resembled the victims he had worked, particularly young Samoan or Pacific Islander men, his chest would tighten and he would feel an urgent need to leave the vicinity. More disturbingly, positive emotions had become destabilizing. When his daughter called with good news, or when a case was solved, the momentary relief or happiness would trigger something chaotic in him—a sense that he was betraying something, or that safety was impossible and he should not allow himself to feel it. These moments of unexpected feeling became triggers themselves, and Marcus found himself increasingly unable to tolerate them.

The memories themselves had become fragmented and intrusive. When Marcus tried to explain to his ex-wife why he had pulled away, why he could no longer attend family gatherings, the words would scatter in his mouth. He would start to describe what he was experiencing and find himself unable to finish, the narrative dissolving into rage so intense he had to leave the room. The memories did not come only when he sought them; they arrived without warning, detonated by a smell or a face glimpsed in a crowded precinct hallway, flooding his consciousness with the full sensory weight of childhood terror—the smell of burnt tobacco, the sound of his own breathing, the certainty that he deserved what was happening to him.

Because Marcus had come to believe something fundamental about himself: that the abuse had revealed his true nature. He was, he was certain, the sort of person to whom terrible things happened, and his reactions since the trauma—the avoidance, the hypervigilance, the rage—proved he was a lousy coper, fundamentally broken in ways that could not be repaired. The world, which he had once believed operated according to rules and justice, had revealed itself as fundamentally arbitrary and malevolent. And so when triggers appeared—the burnt smell, the familiar face, the unexpected surge of relief—Marcus responded by withdrawing further.

He began to avoid wearing clothes similar to what his stepfather had worn, a small measure of control that extended into a broader avoidance of his own body and appearance. He stopped going to crime scenes that involved young men of his ethnicity, calling in favors to reassign cases, a decision that baffled his captain and isolated him further from his team. Most significantly, he began to avoid other people altogether. He took the night shift, worked alone, declined invitations from colleagues. His apartment became smaller, his world contracted. The avoidance provided temporary relief—if he was alone, there was no risk of encountering a trigger, no chance of being flooded with memories, no possibility of the rage that left him ashamed and terrified of his own capacity for violence.

But the relief was illusory. The more Marcus avoided, the more his memories seemed to intensify, as though his detachment from them had somehow made them more vivid, more intrusive. By detaching from the memories, by refusing to engage with them or speak about them, he had inadvertently strengthened their grip. And the avoidance itself became a source of new shame, new evidence that he was failing, that he was weak. His sleep deteriorated further—he lay awake through the small hours, needing to stay alert, unable to surrender to rest because rest meant vulnerability. When he finally did sleep, the memories came as nightmares so vivid he would wake gasping, his body drenched in sweat, his heart hammering as though he were still that terrified child.

Three months ago, Marcus had a panic attack at the precinct. He was reviewing case files when a detective walked past wearing cologne that contained a burnt tobacco note. The smell hit him like a physical blow, and Marcus found himself unable to breathe, unable to move, certain that he was dying. He had to leave the building, and the incident could not be hidden. His captain suggested he take medical leave and consider counseling. Marcus had resisted, but the accumulation of losses—the relationships he had damaged through withdrawal, the cases he could no longer work, the increasing sense that his life was being consumed by something he could not name or control—had finally worn him down. He came to the clinic because he was afraid of what might happen if he did not, and because some part of him, the part that had survived childhood, still believed that understanding the threat might be the first step toward surviving it again.
